modules.summary: The chapter opens with resized photos: some look natural and some look stretched. The learner discovers that a shape is kept only when width and height change by the same multiplying factor, not by the same amount.

media.title: Same Shape, or Just Stretched?
media.context: This is the chapter opener and it plays before any objective. It covers the textbook's opening on scaling that goes wrong, and withholds everything the chapter builds: no ratio is written, no factor is named and no proportion is solved. Students arrive with fractions and multiplication.
media.description: The same tiger photo is stretched wider on a phone while its height stays fixed, making the animal look oddly flat, while a second copy grows in width and height together and remains a proper tiger. The clip then connects this idea to everyday scaling: a noticeboard photograph with squashed faces, a recipe for four incorrectly scaled to six, and two paint mixtures described with the same words but producing different colours, showing that changing dimensions or quantities without preserving the correct proportions can distort the result.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Arouse curiosity about what must be preserved when a quantity is scaled. Key teaching points: 1) Increasing both parts is not enough to preserve a shape. 2) Adding the same amount changes the relationship between the parts. 3) Multiplying both parts by one number does not. 4) The same trap appears in pictures, recipes and mixtures. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often scale by adding rather than by multiplying. 2) Students often assume any increase to both parts is safe. Pause points: 0:29, at the end of and the recipe tasted wrong: ask what the printer did wrong. 1:15, just before the opening question: ask how the recipe should have been scaled. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what stays the same when a photo is enlarged properly. After viewing, ask why adding to both parts changes a mixture.
media.generation_prompt:
INTENT
    Show four careful enlargements all going wrong, so the thing that must stay fixed becomes
    the question, and let one drag ruin a picture while another leaves it alone.

  STORY
    A tiger, a photo, a recipe and a paint mixture all grow correctly and all come out wrong.

  RENDERER
    Manim Community Edition v0.18 or later. Scene subclass.
    1920x1080, 16:9, 30 fps. Default frame is 14.22 x 8 units. All content
    inside a 4 percent safe margin. Nothing cropped.

  CHAPTER VISUAL LANGUAGE, repeat verbatim in every video of this chapter
    Background: dark slate #1F2937.
    Primary object / first set: teal #0072B2.
    Secondary object / second set: amber #E69F00.
    Shared or agreeing: green #009E73.
    Focus or highlight: reddish purple #CC79A7.
    Neutral construction lines, axes, ticks: grey #6B7280.
    Wrong, rejected or impossible case only: muted red #D55E00.
    Text off white. Body 36 px equivalent, labels 28 px.
    Prose uses Text. Mathematics uses MathTex with standard LaTeX only.
    Flat fills, uniform line weights, no gradients or glow.

  ASSETS
    No external files. No image, SVG, font or audio imports. Build everything
    from Manim primitives: Line, Arc, Circle, Polygon, Dot, Arrow, Brace,
    NumberLine, Axes, Table, VGroup.

  MATHEMATICAL TRUTH MODEL
    Every value below is the only value that may appear on screen.
    the first drag: the photo is dragged wider while its height stays put, and the animal turns oddly flat
    the second: the copy grows in width and height together and stays a proper tiger
    the photograph: enlarged for a noticeboard, and the faces come out squashed, though both sides were increased
    the recipe: written for four and scaled to six, and the result tastes wrong although every quantity was raised
    the paint: two mixtures described with the same words, more red and more white, coming out as different colours
    the claim: adding the same amount to both parts is not the same as scaling them
    the consequence: only one of the two keeps the shape or the taste or the colour
    the question: what quiet rule the two edges must obey for a picture to stay itself, and what has to stay fixed when a quantity grows
    what it is not: the difference between the two parts
    withheld: every ratio, every factor, every method, the rule itself and every measurement

  SCENE PLAN
    Total running time 90 seconds across 7 scenes (house-style structure:
    title card, four hook beats, teaser, closing invite).

    Scene 1. Title card. 12 seconds.
      Narration: "Proportional reasoning. Four careful enlargements, every one of them done
      properly, and every one of them wrong."

    Scene 2. Dragged wider, or grown properly. 17 seconds.
      The same tiger photo three times: as it was, dragged wider with its height fixed, and
      grown in width and height together. The first copy turns flat, the second stays a tiger.
      Narration: "The same tiger photo is dragged wider on a phone while its height stays
      exactly where it was, and the animal turns oddly flat. A second copy grows in width and
      in height together, and stays a perfectly proper tiger."

    Scene 3. The faces came out squashed. 14 seconds.
      Narration: "A photograph is enlarged for a noticeboard and the faces come out oddly
      squashed, and yet the printer swears quite honestly that both of the sides were
      increased before it went to press."

    Scene 4. And the recipe tasted wrong. 13 seconds.
      Narration: "A recipe written for four people is scaled up to feed six, and the result
      tastes distinctly wrong, even though every single quantity in it was raised."

    Scene 5. Same words, different colours. 15 seconds.
      Narration: "Two mixtures of paint are described in exactly the same words, more red and
      more white, and they come out as completely different colours. So adding the same amount
      to both parts is not the same thing as scaling them."

    Scene 6. Teaser. 12 seconds.
      Three future-tense promises, each with its own illustration.

    Scene 7. The opening question. 7 seconds.
      Narration: "So what has to stay fixed when a quantity grows? It is plainly not the
      difference. Try the Scaling Grid."

  ANIMATION RULES
    Prefer animation over narration wherever a concept can be shown.
    Every scene contains at least one transformation that carries meaning.
    No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
    Reveal progressively; never dump a finished diagram in one Create.
    On-screen text minimal; no paragraph of prose on screen at any time.
    Objects that persist across scenes are transformed, never recreated.
    No decorative-only animation.

  MATHEMATICAL ACCURACY, highest priority
    100 percent accurate to NCERT Ganita Prakash for Class 8. Correct
    notation, terminology, symbols and labels as used in the Class 8
    textbook. Proportions true wherever proportion carries meaning; if a
    figure is not to scale it must say so on screen. No transformation may
    pass through a mathematically false intermediate state.
    THE STRETCH MUST BE A REAL STRETCH. The "dragged wider" copy must have a
    genuinely different width-to-height ratio from the original, and the
    "grown properly" copy must have EXACTLY the original ratio. A render guard
    asserts both before either is drawn, so the picture cannot lie.

  LANGUAGE
    British spelling. No em dash and no en dash anywhere, in narration or on
    screen. Readable aloud by a student of this grade. Indian names and places
    for any person or setting.

  NEGATIVE CONSTRAINTS
    No value, label or claim absent from the truth model.
    No rule, formula, method or answer from any later part of the chapter.
    Nothing is taught here; the film only opens questions.
    No ratio is written, no scale factor is named, no measurement is given.
    No text outside the safe margin, no overlapping labels.
    No external assets, watermarks or branding.
    No particles, sparkles or glow.

  SELF-CHECK BEFORE OUTPUT
    1. Scene durations sum to about 90 seconds.
    2. Every number, count and label on screen appears in the truth model and nowhere else.
       (Only "four" and "six", from the recipe, are permitted.)
    3. Every mobject named in a beat is declared in the inventory before it is used.
    4. Every persisting mobject is transformed into its next form, never recreated.
    5. No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
    6. All geometry lies within x in [-6.8, 6.8] and y in [-3.8, 3.8]; nothing is cropped.
    7. No label overlaps another label; buff at least 0.2 everywhere.
    8. British spelling throughout, and no em dash or en dash in narration or on screen.
    9. Nothing in the film teaches a rule or reveals a later result.
    10. The film closes on curiosity about the chapter, and the named tool (the Scaling Grid)
        is handed to the student in the closing narration.

media.title: Same factor keeps the shape
labels: the same factor, so the shape is kept
different factors, so the shape is lost
media.context: A picture keeps its shape only when both dimensions are multiplied by the same factor, and taking the same amount off both does not do it. The worked example resizes an 80 mm by 50 mm photo to 40 mm by 25 mm and asks whether the shape is kept. The figure computes both factors and sets a subtracting resize beside it.
media.description: Same factor keeps the shape: a labelled figure illustrating the idea, drawn from the worked example 'A photo is 80 mm wide and 50 mm tall. It is resized to 40 mm by 25 mm. Does it keep its shape?'.

source_image.alt: Diagram for same factor keeps the shape.
source_image.caption: Same factor keeps the shape: a labelled figure illustrating the idea, drawn from the worked example 'A photo is 80 mm wide and 50 mm tall. It is resized to 40 mm by 25 mm. Does it keep its shape?'.

media.teaching_notes: Ask whether taking the same amount off both sides keeps the shape; most classes say yes. Computing both factors settles it. Then resize by a factor of their choosing and check both dimensions.
media.negative_prompt: photorealistic rendering, photographic texture, 3D modelling, isometric or perspective projection, drop shadows, gradients, glossy or metallic surfaces, neon glow; decorative clutter, background scenery, ornamental borders, frames, mascots, emoji, speech bubbles that carry no information; watermarks, signatures, logos, stock imagery, colour swatches; garbled or misspelled words, invented digits, duplicated or contradictory labels, handwriting and script fonts, wording in any script other than English; text cropped at the edge, labels overlapping the figure, type too small to read at half size; any wording at all beyond the listed labels, including added titles, captions, summaries, or a sentence describing what the figure shows; a resized rectangle whose drawn proportions contradict its labels; a factor that is arithmetically wrong; the subtracting resize shown as keeping the shape; an overlay that matches when the factors differ; the failing case drawn without its cross
media.generation_prompt: Flat educational vector illustration in the style of an NCERT Grade 8 mathematics textbook: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines, a restrained palette of one teal accent, one amber accent and neutral grey, flat fills with no shading and no gradients, all wording in a clean sans-serif, 16:9 landscape at 1456 by 816 pixels. Scene: The original photo is drawn at the left as a rectangle 80 mm wide and 50 mm tall with both dimensions marked. Two resized versions run to the right. The first, ticked in a teal circle, is 40 mm by 25 mm with factor strips beneath reading '40 divided by 80 = one half' and '25 divided by 50 = one half', tagged the same factor, and an overlay showing the small rectangle scaled up to sit exactly on the original outline. The second, crossed in a red circle, is 60 mm by 30 mm made by taking 20 mm off each side, with factor strips reading '60 divided by 80 = 0.75' and '30 divided by 50 = 0.6', tagged different factors, and an overlay showing it failing to match the original outline when scaled. Draw no wording at all except the following, which is the complete and only text in the figure, spelled exactly like this: 80 mm; 50 mm; 40 mm; 25 mm; 40 divided by 80 = one half; 25 divided by 50 = one half; the same factor, so the shape is kept; 60 mm; 30 mm; 0.75; 0.6; different factors, so the shape is lost.
media.accuracy_constraints:
The ticked resize must have both factors equal to one half, drawn in true proportion.
The crossed resize must have factors of 0.75 and 0.6, visibly different.
The overlay for the ticked case must match the original outline exactly and the crossed case must not.
Every factor shown must be the resized dimension divided by the original.
The subtracting resize must be marked as failing.
Every number, count and label drawn in the figure must match this brief exactly; no value may be invented, rounded or added.
Use NCERT Ganita Prakash Grade 8 wording for every term, keep British spelling, and write no sentence that a Grade 8 reader could not read aloud.

media.title: Scale Figure Stretcher
media.context: CBSE Class 8, Ganita Prakash Part 1, Chapter 7 Proportional Reasoning, section 7.1 Observing Similarity in Change. This tool OPENS the chapter: it is read before ratio notation is formalised in 7.2 and long before the term scale factor arrives in Part 2, so the controls are named Width factor and Height factor and the condition is stated as 'both sides multiplied by the same factor'. The textbook's own hook is a set of resized digital images, where dragging a corner keeps the picture and pulling one side elongates it; this mount is that hook made testable.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer, and the side ratios that explain it.
whatYouLearned: A figure keeps its shape exactly when both sides are multiplied by the same factor
Matching sides of figures of the same shape are in the same ratio
Adding the same amount to each side is not enlarging, because it changes the ratio
A common factor below 1 keeps the shape just as well as one above 1

overview.goal: The student scales a figure so it keeps its shape, identifies which changes distort it, and states the condition for shape preservation.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A unit grid on a plain working ground, with the figure's original outline left behind as a faint ghost. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class says a figure that has only been made wider is still the same shape, and the two side ratios are asked to settle it.
overview.concept: A figure keeps its shape when width and height are multiplied by the same factor. Multiplying by different factors stretches it, and adding the same amount to each side does not preserve shape either, because adding changes the ratio between the sides.
overview.purpose: The student scales a figure so it keeps its shape, identifies which changes distort it, and states the condition for shape preservation.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Figure fills the main panel with both sliders beneath and the ratio readouts to the right on a wide frame and under the sliders on a 390 px frame. Slider handles keep a 44 px hit target. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not show the shape indicator while a prediction is still open, and never derive it from the slider lock. An indicator that trusts the lock would teach the wrong condition.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Shape is decided by the ratio between the sides, not by their lengths. Multiplying both sides by the same factor leaves that ratio untouched, because the factor cancels. Multiplying by different factors changes the ratio, and adding a constant changes it too, since a constant is a different proportion of a short side than of a long one. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.summary: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item sets the two scale factors from its own numbers, shows the question, then reveals the scaled figure, the side ratios and the answer together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): The condition is that the two factors are equal, not that the figure changed. Breaks: Believing a shape test needs a visible change before it can be passed. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): A common factor below 1 preserves shape too; the condition says equal, not larger. Breaks: Believing only an enlargement can keep the shape. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): Adding a fixed amount changes the ratio, because that amount is a bigger share of the shorter side. Breaks: Enlargement understood as adding a fixed amount to each side rather than multiplying. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): The condition is exact equality of the two factors; nearly equal is a different shape. Breaks: Believing a small difference between the two factors still counts as the same shape. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): One case where a wrong rule happens to work does not make it a rule. Breaks: Generalising from the square, where adding equal amounts happens to leave the ratio at 1 to 1.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the figure at its original size with both factors at 1 and the shape indicator hidden, and ask the class to say out loud whether doubling the width alone keeps the shape. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Targets: width factor 1, height factor 1. Never move a slider before the prediction is committed and never show the indicator at this call. Call 2. Set the width factor to 2 with the height factor left at 1, and point at the two side ratios as they part. Targets: width factor 2, height factor 1. Read both ratios from the tool's own readout and never from this plan. Call 3. Set the height factor to 2 as well so the two factors agree, and point at the shape indicator as it comes back on. Targets: width factor 2, height factor 2. State the condition only after the indicator has turned on.

hunts: EQUAL FACTOR HUNT: find three pairs of factors that keep the shape and three that do not, then say what the passing pairs share.
SHRINK TEST: find a common factor below 1 and say whether the indicator behaves any differently from an enlargement.
ADDING TRAP: find the one kind of figure whose shape survives adding the same amount to both sides.
NEAR MISS: move one slider by the smallest step you can and find where the indicator goes off.

observationsAndConclusions.why: The two side ratios stop agreeing as soon as the two factors differ
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The shape indicator goes off the moment one slider moves on its own
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Shape is decided by the ratio between the sides, not by how large the figure is

observationsAndConclusions.why: A common factor cancels out of the ratio whether it is above 1 or below it
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Both factors set to one half keeps the indicator on
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Shrinking preserves shape exactly as enlarging does; the condition says equal, not larger

observationsAndConclusions.why: The added amount is a larger share of the shorter side, so it only leaves the ratio alone when the sides were already equal
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Adding the same amount to both sides moves the ratio on every figure except a square
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: One figure on which a wrong rule happens to work does not turn it into a rule

media.description: A rectangle stands on a unit grid with its original outline held behind it as a faint ghost, and BOTH of the tests the textbook uses are printed and separately labelled: the factor of change on each side (new divided by old, written as a fraction with its decimal beside it) and the width : height ratio in simplest form, before and after. They are different numbers, and mixing them is the commonest way this topic is taught wrongly. Three refutations are drawn rather than asserted. A same-shape ray runs from the origin through the original's far corner, and the scaled figure's corner sits on it exactly when the shape survives - inward as well as outward, so a common factor below one lands on it too. An inscribed circle becomes an obvious oval the moment the two factors part. An additive control grows both sides by the same LENGTH and visibly walks the corner off the ray, which is the additive reading of enlargement refuted rather than merely excluded. The shape indicator is computed from the two factors and never from the slider lock, so locking cannot fake a preserved shape, and a near miss such as 2 against 2.1 turns it off with the factor gap and the tolerance of 0.05 both on screen, so how close is not close enough is a stated threshold rather than a hidden one.

scenes.onScreen: The figure, both sliders, the ratios, the indicator, every control, no score and no question. A 3 by 5 figure at scale 1 with both sliders free and every control live.
scenes.animation: Stretch: the figure deforms continuously with the ghost outline held, so the distortion is measured against the original rather than remembered.
scenes.interaction: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.
scenes.valuesShown: Every readout stays live, so the invariants keep being computed while the student explores

concept.notation: A scale factor multiplies a length. Two figures have the same shape when every pair of matching sides is in the same ratio.
concept.statement: A figure keeps its shape when width and height are multiplied by the same factor. Multiplying by different factors stretches it, and adding the same amount to each side does not preserve shape either, because adding changes the ratio between the sides.
prerequisites: reading a scale factor as a multiplier
misconceptions: Enlargement understood as adding a fixed amount to each side rather than multiplying.
Shape assumed preserved under any stretch, so a wider figure is still called the same shape.
concept.why_it_is_true: Shape is decided by the ratio between the sides, not by their lengths. Multiplying both sides by the same factor leaves that ratio untouched, because the factor cancels. Multiplying by different factors changes the ratio, and adding a constant changes it too, since a constant is a different proportion of a short side than of a long one.
worked_numbers: A 3 by 5 figure scaled by 2 in both directions becomes 6 by 10, and both ratios read 3 to 5.
Scaled by 2 in width only it becomes 6 by 5, and the ratio moves from 3 to 5 to 6 to 5.
Adding 2 to each side gives 5 by 7, whose ratio is 5 to 7 and not 3 to 5.

lockSlidersOutcomes.on: both factors move as one, and the indicator is still computed from the ratios
lockSlidersOutcomes.off: the two factors move independently, so the ratios can be parted

setWidthScaleOutcomes.1: the figure is left at its original width
setWidthScaleOutcomes.2: the figure doubles across; with the height still at 1 the indicator goes off
setWidthScaleOutcomes.3: the widest stretch the tool draws
setWidthScaleOutcomes.0.5: the figure halves across and the width ratio reads one half
setWidthScaleOutcomes.1.5: the figure widens by half again and the two ratios part unless the height matches

answer_key.worked: A figure keeps its shape exactly when both scale factors are equal, because that is what leaves the side ratio unchanged.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn figure: both side ratios, whether they agree within the stated tolerance, and the two scale factors.
answer_key.precision: Ratios are compared with a stated tolerance which is displayed on screen. Slider steps are chosen so the ratio display never becomes a repeating decimal.
answer_key.ground_truth: sideRatios(figure) = the ratio of each pair of matching sides. shapePreserved(original, scaled) = every pair of ratios agrees within tolerance. scaleFactors(original, scaled) = the width and height multipliers.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The figure is unchanged and the shape is preserved. This is the trivial case and the tool keeps the indicator on rather than treating no change as no answer.
The indicator stays on at any common factor, including factors below 1, so shrinking is shown to preserve shape just as enlarging does.

edge_cases.case: A near miss, such as 2 and 2.1
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The indicator goes off and the tolerance is displayed, so the student can see how close is not close enough rather than guessing at the threshold.
The indicator is still computed from the side ratios and never from the lock state, so locking cannot fake a preserved shape.

edge_cases.case: An added amount rather than a multiplier
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Offered as an alternative control and shown to break the ratio, so the additive strategy is refuted here as well as in the mixer.

constraints: The shape preserved indicator is computed from the side ratios and never from the slider lock state, so locking cannot produce a false positive.
Ratios are compared with a tolerance that is displayed on screen, so a near miss is a stated threshold rather than a hidden one.
Slider steps are chosen to avoid repeating decimals in the ratio display, so the numbers stay readable.
The additive control is available and shown to break the ratio, so the misconception is refuted rather than merely excluded.
The figure is redrawn from the original vertices at each scale, so repeated scaling cannot accumulate rounding drift.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example setting a scale pair a child names and letting the ratios decide.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a predict verb in windowMethods

teaching_notes: Beat 1 states the idea with the case that works: a 3 by 5 figure with both factors at 2 becomes 6 by 10, the corner lands on the ray, and the width : height ratio reads 3 : 5 both before and after. Ask the class out loud, BEFORE reading the screen, whether doubling the width alone would do the same - the guess is what makes beat 2 worth watching.

Beat 2 is the mechanism. The width factor alone moves to 2 and the height factor stays at 1, so the ratio walks from 3 : 5 to 6 : 5, the inscribed circle becomes an oval and the corner leaves the ray by a stated number of grid units. Point at the two factor chips as they part; the picture and the numbers are saying the same thing at the same moment.

Beat 3 closes the commonest gap: the condition says EQUAL, not LARGER. Both factors go to one half, the figure shrinks to 1.5 by 2.5, the corner lands back on the ray between the origin and the original corner, and the indicator comes back on. Never say a doubled figure is 'twice as big' - each side is twice as long, and it covers four grid squares for every one.

media.title: The Secret Is One Shared Factor
media.context: This hook opens the topic on the shared factor. Students have seen the tiger. The film must not name the factor and must not state the rule.
media.description: Two rectangles sit side by side. One has both sides doubled and looks like the original, while the other has the same length added to each side and looks squashed. Adding equal amounts is not the same as multiplying by equal factors.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: See that a shape is preserved when both dimensions are multiplied by the same factor. Key teaching points: 1) Doubling both sides preserves the shape. 2) Adding the same amount to both sides does not. 3) The preserved quantity is the factor, not the difference. 4) That factor is shared by every dimension. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often add equally and expect the shape to survive. 2) Students often think a larger figure must be a different shape. Pause points: 0:24, at the end of not the same thing: ask what number both sides of the good rectangle were multiplied by. 0:24, just before the open question: ask why adding two to each side failed. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what stays the same when both sides double. After viewing, ask what a shared factor means.

    Secondary object / second set: amber #E69F00.
    Shared or agreeing: green #009E73.
    Focus or highlight: reddish purple #CC79A7.
    Neutral construction lines, axes, ticks: grey #6B7280.
    Wrong, rejected or impossible case only: muted red #D55E00.
    Text off white. Body 36 px equivalent, labels 28 px.
    Prose uses Text. Mathematics uses MathTex with standard LaTeX only.
    Flat fills, uniform line weights, no gradients or glow.

  ASSETS
    No external files. No image, SVG, font or audio imports. Build everything
    from Manim primitives: Line, Arc, Circle, Polygon, Dot, Arrow, Brace,
    NumberLine, Axes, Table, VGroup.

  MATHEMATICAL TRUTH MODEL
    Every value below is the only value that may appear on screen.
    the original: a rectangle of 4 by 3
    the first change: both sides doubled, giving 8 by 6, which looks like the original
    the second change: the same length added to each side, giving 6 by 5, which looks squashed
    the claim: adding equal amounts is not the same as multiplying by equal factors
    withheld: the name of the shared number, and the rule

  SCENE PLAN
    Total running time 35 seconds across 3 scenes.

    Scene 1. Doubled, and added to
      Duration: 14 seconds.
      On screen at the start: an empty dark slate frame.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  Write(s1_caption) over 0.9 s, to set the frame of the scene.
      at 2.1 s  Create(s1_fig0) over 1.2 s, lag_ratio 0.3, to draw figure 1 side by side.
      at 4.3 s  Write(s1_fig0labels) over 1.0 s, lag_ratio 0.2, to label figure 1.
      at 6.3 s  Create(s1_fig1) over 1.2 s, lag_ratio 0.3, to draw figure 2 side by side.
      at 8.6 s  Write(s1_fig1labels) over 1.0 s, lag_ratio 0.2, to label figure 2.
      at 10.6 s  FadeIn(s1_fignote) over 0.8 s, to state the observation the scene has just made.
      at 12.4 s  FadeOut(s1_fig0, s1_fig0labels, s1_fig1, s1_fig1labels, s1_fignote) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "Two rectangles sit side by side. One has both of its sides doubled and looks just like the original, and the other has the same length added to each side."
      Persists into the next scene: s1_caption.

    Scene 2. Not the same thing
      Duration: 10 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s1_caption.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  ReplacementTransform(s1_caption, s2_caption) over 0.9 s, to carry the caption forward rather than redrawing it.
      at 1.5 s  Write(s2_left) over 0.9 s, to put up the first quantity.
      at 2.9 s  Write(s2_right) over 0.9 s, to put up the second quantity.
      at 4.2 s  FadeIn(s2_rel) over 0.6 s, to leave the relation between them undecided.
      at 5.2 s  FadeIn(s2_complabels) over 0.8 s, lag_ratio 0.2, to name what each side stands for.
      at 6.5 s  Indicate(s2_rel) over 0.8 s, to press on the undecided sign.
      at 7.7 s  FadeIn(s2_cnote) over 0.8 s, to state the observation the scene has just made.
      at 9.0 s  FadeOut(s2_left, s2_right, s2_rel, s2_complabels, s2_cnote) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "And that second one looks squashed. So adding equal amounts is plainly not the same thing as multiplying by equal factors at all."
      Persists into the next scene: s2_caption.

    Scene 3. The open question
      Duration: 11 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s2_caption.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  AddTextLetterByLetter(s3_question) over 1.8 s, to let the question land word by word.
      at 3.6 s  Create(s3_rule) over 0.6 s, to underline the question.
      at 5.8 s  FadeIn(s3_qsub) over 0.7 s, to name where the student will go looking.
      at 8.0 s  Circumscribe(s3_question) over 1.4 s, to hold the question as the closing image.
      Narration: "So which single number do both edges have to share for the shape to survive? Spot it for yourself on the Scaling Grid."
      Persists into the next scene: nothing, this is the last scene.

  ANIMATION RULES
    Prefer animation over narration wherever a concept can be shown.
    Every scene contains at least one transformation that carries meaning.
    No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
    Reveal progressively; never dump a finished diagram in one Create.
    On-screen text minimal; no paragraph of prose on screen at any time.
    Objects that persist across scenes are transformed, never recreated.
    No decorative-only animation.

  MATHEMATICAL ACCURACY, highest priority
    100 percent accurate to NCERT Ganita Prakash for Class 8. Correct
    notation, terminology, symbols and labels as used in the Class 8
    textbook. Proportions true wherever proportion carries meaning; if a
    figure is not to scale it must say so on screen. No transformation may
    pass through a mathematically false intermediate state.

  LANGUAGE
    British spelling. No em dash and no en dash anywhere, in narration or on
    screen. Readable aloud by a student of this grade. Indian names and places
    for any person or setting.

  NEGATIVE CONSTRAINTS
    No value, label or claim absent from the truth model.
    No revealing of the rule, formula or answer anywhere in this hook.
    No worked solution, no general statement of the method.
    No text outside the safe margin, no overlapping labels.
    No external assets, watermarks or branding.
    No particles, sparkles or glow.

  SELF-CHECK BEFORE OUTPUT
    1. Scene durations sum to exactly 35 seconds across 3 scenes.
    2. Every number, count and label on screen appears in the truth model and nowhere else.
    3. Every mobject named in a beat is declared in the inventory before it is used.
    4. Every persisting mobject is transformed into its next form, never recreated.
    5. No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
    6. All geometry lies within x in [-6.8, 6.8] and y in [-3.8, 3.8]; nothing is cropped.
    7. No label overlaps another label; buff at least 0.2 everywhere.
    8. British spelling throughout, and no em dash or en dash in narration or on screen.
    9. The final frame is the open question, with no rule, method or answer shown.
    10. The named tool is handed to the student in the closing narration.

topics.summary: A picture keeps its shape only when width and height change by the same factor. Removing the same amount from each side gives different factors and distorts it. The learner compares the width factor with the height factor to predict similar or distorted.

content.text: A picture keeps its shape when its width and its height are both multiplied by the same number. That number is called the factor of change. If the width is halved, the height must also be halved for the picture to look the same. Taking away the same amount, like 20 mm from each side, does not keep the shape, because the same amount is a different factor for a small side than for a large side. To decide, find the width factor and the height factor and see whether they are equal. Changes that share one factor are called proportional.

Scene: A rack is drawn holding 8 footballs on an upper shelf and 2 basketballs on a lower shelf, each counted and labelled. A ratio card beneath reads '8 : 2' with its two numbers tagged as the terms, and a reading strip reads that this means 8 footballs for every 2 basketballs. A grouping overlay divides the footballs into 2 equal groups of 4, one matched to each basketball, with a division strip reading '8 divided by 2 = 4' and a result card reading four times as many footballs. A simplest form note reads that 8 : 2 is the same as 4 : 1. Draw no wording at all except the following, which is the complete and only text in the figure, spelled exactly like this: 8 footballs; 2 basketballs; 8 : 2; the terms; 8 for every 2; 8 divided by 2 = 4; four times as many footballs; 8 : 2 is the same as 4 : 1.

The rack must hold exactly 8 footballs and 2 basketballs.
The ratio must read 8 : 2, in the order footballs to basketballs.
The grouping must show 2 equal groups of 4 footballs, one per basketball.
The multiple must be 4, from 8 divided by 2.
The simplest form must be given as 4 : 1.
Every number, count and label drawn in the figure must match this brief exactly; no value may be invented, rounded or added.

media.title: Ratio Mixer
media.context: CBSE Class 8, Ganita Prakash Ch.7 'Proportional Reasoning', §7.2 Ratios and §7.3 Ratios in Their Simplest Form. This is the chapter's central contrast: additive and multiplicative reasoning are put side by side on ONE pair of glasses, before any proportion machinery is introduced. Notation is the colon (2 : 3) throughout, the multiplier is called the FACTOR OF CHANGE (the textbook's own name), and the blackboard leads with the simplest form and the factor of change and gives the cross products as the confirming line — cross multiplication is a check in this chapter, not the taught route. Zero terms are a convention of THIS mixer, not a theorem of mathematics: NCERT does not discuss them.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's mixture, the correct one, and the swatches that explain it.
whatYouLearned: A mixture is decided by the ratio of its parts, not by how much of it there is
Multiplying both parts by the same number keeps the mixture exactly
Adding the same amount to both parts changes the mixture, however fair it looks
Two mixtures are equal exactly when their terms cross multiply to the same product

overview.goal: The student changes both quantities so the mixture stays the same and states the operation that preserves it.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain counter with two glasses drawn as stacked unit blocks and a solid colour swatch above each. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class says that adding one spoon of concentrate and one spoon of water keeps the drink tasting exactly the same, and the two swatches are asked to settle it.
overview.concept: A mixture is decided by the ratio of its two parts and not by their totals. Multiplying both parts by the same number keeps the ratio and therefore the taste. Adding the same amount to both changes the ratio, because the same amount is a different share of a small part than of a large one, so the taste changes.
overview.purpose: The student changes both quantities so the mixture stays the same and states the operation that preserves it.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Glasses side by side in the main panel with their swatches above and the block controls beneath. On a 390 px frame the glasses narrow but stay side by side, because the comparison needs both visible. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not show the reduced ratios while a prediction is still open, and never derive a swatch from the totals. A swatch that follows volume would destroy the entire contrast.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Doubling both parts doubles the whole, so each part keeps the same share of the mixture and the shade cannot move. Adding one to each keeps the difference between the parts but changes their ratio, because a fixed amount is proportionally larger for the smaller part. The swatch is computed from the ratio alone, which is why it exposes the difference immediately. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

scenes.subGoal: A zero concentrate is a real mixture, and the swatch still follows the ratio.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): A zero concentrate is a real mixture, and the swatch still follows the ratio. Breaks: Believing a ratio needs both parts to be present before it means anything. ML2 (Medium, Conceptual): Adding the same amount to both parts keeps the difference and destroys the ratio. Breaks: The additive strategy applied to a proportional situation. ML3 (Medium, Edge Case): The mixture is fixed by the ratio, so a bigger glass can hold exactly the same drink. Breaks: Judging a mixture by its total volume rather than by the ratio of its parts. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): The two zero cases are not symmetric: no concentrate is a drink, no water is not a mixture at all. Breaks: Treating the two parts of a ratio as interchangeable when one of them is zero. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): The additive move works in exactly one family of cases, which is why it looks convincing. Breaks: Generalising from an equal parts glass, where adding to both happens to keep the ratio.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on two matching glasses at the same mixture with both swatches shown and no reduced ratios printed, and ask the class to say out loud whether adding one spoon of concentrate and one spoon of water to the right glass keeps the taste. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Target: glass B. Never change a glass before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Add one block to each part of glass B and hold the two swatches side by side so the gap between the shades is visible. Target: glass B, add one to both. Read the new ratio from the tool's own readout and never from this plan. Call 3. Reset glass B and multiply both of its parts by 2 instead, then point at the swatch as the stack grows beneath it. Targets: glass B, multiply both by 2. Name the operation that preserved the mixture only after the swatch has been seen holding still.

media.description: Two glasses stand on one counter, each drawn as a stack of unit blocks with the concentrate always at the bottom and always in the same colour, and above them a single taste bar split into two halves that TOUCH. The colour of each half is computed from that glass's reduced ratio alone and never from its totals, so two glasses of different sizes holding the same mixture paint one unbroken colour and the seam between the halves simply disappears; the moment the two mixtures differ, a seam appears across the bar. Adding one block to each part of a glass is always allowed, and it opens that seam while the difference between the parts is still 1 — which is the additive strategy failing in front of the class. Multiplying both parts holds the colour perfectly still while the stack visibly grows. Every comparison is settled on exact integers by cross multiplication, so a very close but unequal mixture is reported as different rather than as near enough, and the chapter's own factor of change is printed beside the simplest forms. A glass with no concentrate is a real mixture drawn as plain water; a glass with no water is refused, with the reason on screen.

mods.learn: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item sets both glasses from its own numbers, shows the question, then reveals the swatches, the reduced ratios and the answer together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
mods.ai_demo: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with two matching glasses and asks whether adding one spoon of each to one of them keeps the taste. Beat 2 adds one to each and the swatches visibly part, so the additive strategy fails in front of the class. Beat 3 doubles both parts instead and the swatches match again, so multiplying is identified as the operation that preserves the mixture. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setGlass, addToBoth, multiplyBoth and say.
mods.practice: Practice, student operated. The bank from props.questions, one item at a time, each rendering its own glasses. Build an equivalent mixture, judge whether two mixtures match, or name the operation used. Scored, with a star finish and a Review phase that walks every item showing the student's mixture, the correct one and the swatches that settle it.
mods.free_play: Free Play, student operated. The student adds or removes blocks from either glass, compares with the target, and watches the swatches. Nothing is scored and nothing is mandatory.

scenes.interaction: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.
scenes.valuesShown: Every readout stays live, so the invariants keep being computed while the student explores

concept.notation: A mixture is written as concentrate to water, for example 2 to 3. Two mixtures taste the same when their ratios are equivalent.
concept.statement: A mixture is decided by the ratio of its two parts and not by their totals. Multiplying both parts by the same number keeps the ratio and therefore the taste. Adding the same amount to both changes the ratio, because the same amount is a different share of a small part than of a large one, so the taste changes.
misconceptions: The additive strategy applied to a proportional situation, so adding one to each part is expected to keep the mixture.
Judging a mixture by its total volume rather than by the ratio of its parts.
concept.why_it_is_true: Doubling both parts doubles the whole, so each part keeps the same share of the mixture and the shade cannot move. Adding one to each keeps the difference between the parts but changes their ratio, because a fixed amount is proportionally larger for the smaller part. The swatch is computed from the ratio alone, which is why it exposes the difference immediately.
worked_numbers: 2 concentrate to 3 water doubled is 4 to 6, and the shades match.
2 to 3 with one added to each is 3 to 4, and the shade is visibly stronger.
4 to 6 reduces to 2 to 3, so a bigger glass can hold the same mixture.

answer_key.worked: Multiplying both parts by the same number keeps the mixture; adding the same amount to both changes it.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn glasses: the reduced ratio of each, and whether the two are equivalent by cross multiplication.
answer_key.precision: The swatch is computed from the exact reduced ratio, and mixtures are compared by cross multiplication of integers, never by comparing decimal shades.
answer_key.ground_truth: reduced(c, w) = the ratio divided by its highest common factor. equivalent(g1, g2) = c1 times w2 equals c2 times w1, as exact integers. swatch(c, w) = a colour derived from the reduced ratio only.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Blocked with the reason on screen, because a ratio to zero has no meaning here and the swatch would be undefined.
Allowed and drawn as plain water, with the ratio 0 to n stated. It is the boundary case that shows the swatch really does follow the ratio.

edge_cases.case: Two glasses with different totals but the same ratio
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The swatches match exactly, which is the whole point, and the tool says the totals differ while the mixture does not.

edge_cases.case: Adding the same amount to both
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Allowed, and the swatch moves. The tool never blocks the additive move, because watching it fail is the argument.

edge_cases.case: A ratio that does not reduce
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Shown in its own terms with the reduction stated as already simplest, so simplest form is a result rather than a required step.

glassB.description: The second glass, as concentrate and water block counts.

questions.description: Replaces the built in practice bank. Items are {kind:'build_equivalent', c:number, w:number} | {kind:'do_they_match', g1:number[], g2:number[]} | {kind:'name_operation'} | {kind:'choice', prompt, options[], correct, explain}.

showReducedRatio.description: Print each glass's reduced ratio. Off until the student has predicted, since the reduced form gives the comparison away.

constraints: The swatch colour is computed from the exact reduced ratio only, never from the totals, so two glasses of different sizes with the same mixture look identical.
Mixtures are compared by cross multiplication of integers, never by comparing decimal shades, so no rounding decides an equivalence.
A glass with no water is blocked with the reason on screen, since the swatch would be undefined.
The additive move is always available and never blocked, because watching it fail is the chapter's central argument.
Block counts are capped at 12 per part so both glasses stay legible on a 390 px frame.

extra.concept_only: Concept carries no questions of its own. Its beats reveal the idea and then run one reasoning beat each, and every number the agent says is read from state.truth.

ai.shows: Both glasses as stacked blocks, both swatches, the teacher caption, and discrete step navigation (Prev / Step k of 3 / Next) with a progress bar.
steps: Predict: two matching glasses stand side by side. The class commits whether adding one spoon of each to one glass keeps the taste, out loud, and the teacher commits it on the pad. prediction_made unlocks the beat.
Add one each: the second glass changes and its swatch visibly parts from the first.
Double instead: both parts of the second glass are doubled and the swatches match again.

normal.shows: Both glasses, both swatches, every control, no score and no question.

normal.done_when: The student presses Finish, which emits finished once.

play_modes: SAME SHADE HUNT: build three glasses of different sizes whose swatches match exactly, then say what the three share.
ADD ONE TO EACH: find the only kind of glass whose taste survives adding one block to each part.
BLOCKED GLASS: find the one setting the tool refuses, and say why the swatch could not be drawn.
STRONGEST FIRST: build four glasses and put them in order of strength without looking at the swatches.
normal.parameter_freedom: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example running a change a child proposes and letting the swatch answer.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

steps: Take a glass of a concentrate to b water and add one to each part.
Cross multiply the old against the new: a times the quantity b plus 1.
The other product is b times the quantity a plus 1.
Those two agree only when a and b are equal.
So a glass of 5 to 5 survives the move and a glass of 2 to 5 does not.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to make the guess public before any evidence lands. Both glasses hold 2 : 3 and the bar is one unbroken colour; the class says out loud whether one spoon of each into glass B keeps the taste. Commit that answer with predict() before changing a single block — resolving first throws away the only moment the misconception is on the record.

Beat 2 is the argument. One block joins each part of glass B, the seam opens across the bar, and the difference between B's parts is STILL 1 — say that out loud while pointing at it, because 'the gap did not change' is exactly the reason the class believed the move was safe. Only then read the two cross products, 8 and 9, off the tool.

Beat 3 is the same glass rebuilt by multiplying instead. The stack grows to ten blocks and the seam vanishes: the bar reads as one colour again. Name the operation only AFTER the class has watched the colour hold still, and use the textbook's phrase — the factor of change is 2.
media.generation_prompt: Ratio Mixer: two glasses of concentrate and water as stacked blocks with a colour swatch above each, where only multiplying both parts keeps the shades identical
media.instructions_for_student: A mixture is decided by the ratio of its two parts, not by how much of it there is. Build a glass by adding or removing concentrate and water blocks, and watch the taste bar above it. When two glasses hold the same mixture their halves of the bar become one unbroken colour, with no seam between them. Multiply BOTH parts by the same number and the colour will not move, however big the glass gets. Add the same amount to both parts and it will — even though that feels fair.

Scene: Two bar pairs are drawn one above the other. The upper pair shows 4 units against 5 units, labelled 4 : 5, with the two bars drawn in proportion. A scaling arrow labelled multiply both terms by 3 leads to the lower pair, showing 12 units against 15 units, labelled 12 : 15, drawn longer but in the same proportion, with a matching shape overlay confirming the comparison is unchanged. Two scaling strips read '4 x 3 = 12' and '5 x 3 = 15'. A crossed out note shows only the first term scaled, giving 12 : 5, tagged as a different relationship. A tag reads that dividing both terms by the same number works the same way. Draw no wording at all except the following, which is the complete and only text in the figure, spelled exactly like this: 4 : 5; multiply both terms by 3; 4 x 3 = 12; 5 x 3 = 15; 12 : 15; the same relationship; not 12 : 5; dividing both terms works the same way.
media.accuracy_constraints:
Both terms must be multiplied by the same factor of 3, giving 12 : 15.
Both bar pairs must be drawn in true proportion to their ratios.
The proportion must be visibly unchanged between the two pairs.
The one term slip giving 12 : 5 must be crossed.
The note must state that dividing both terms also works.
Every number, count and label drawn in the figure must match this brief exactly; no value may be invented, rounded or added.
Use NCERT Ganita Prakash Grade 8 wording for every term, keep British spelling, and write no sentence that a Grade 8 reader could not read aloud.

media.title: Ratio Table Filler
media.context: CBSE Class 8, NCERT Ganita Prakash Ch.7 Proportional Reasoning-1, §7.1 Observing Similarity in Change — ratios written a : b, simplest form by the HCF, and the book's own phrase 'factor of change' for the multiplier between two entries. It sits after the mixer, where the same preserving operation is written down as a table so it can be used to FIND values rather than only to compare them. Cross multiplication is a formal step at this grade, so it is drawn rather than described. It is read before any similarity or unitary-method result later in the chapter, and it rehearses the 1-mark 'is this column equivalent' reading and the 2-mark missing-entry item directly.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.

whatYouLearned: A column belongs in a ratio table only when both entries were multiplied or divided by the same number

overview.goal: The student completes a ratio table by multiplying or dividing both entries, names the operation used, and rejects row operations that break the ratio.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A two row table laid across the working ground with labelled arrows arcing between adjacent columns. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class continues a ratio table by carrying on the pattern along the top row, and the base ratio is asked whether the new column still belongs.
overview.concept: A column of a ratio table stays equivalent to the base ratio only if both entries are multiplied or divided by the same number. Adding a constant to one row, or different numbers to the two rows, produces a column that is no longer in the ratio, and the drift can be measured.
overview.purpose: The student completes a ratio table by multiplying or dividing both entries, names the operation used, and rejects row operations that break the ratio.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Table across the main panel with the base ratio pinned to the left. On a 390 px frame the table scrolls horizontally and the arrows scroll with it, so a label never separates from its columns. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not fill any blank while a prediction is still open, and never accept a column that is not equivalent to the base. An accepted bad column would teach that the table is a pattern rather than a ratio.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Multiplying both entries by the same number leaves the ratio unchanged, because the multiplier cancels between the two. Adding leaves the difference unchanged instead, which is a different invariant and not the one a ratio is about. Labelling the arrow forces the operation into the open, so a right number reached by an additive route is caught. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Conceptual): A table is a ratio, not a pattern, so a column has to be earned by multiplying. Breaks: Filling a table by continuing an additive pattern along the rows. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): The multiplier between columns may be a fraction, and the column is still exact. Breaks: Believing a ratio table only works when one column divides into the next. ML3 (Medium, Edge Case): A correct entry can arrive with a wrong account of how it was made, and the account is graded too. Breaks: Believing a right number proves a right method. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): The ratio holds between any two columns, not only between neighbours. Breaks: Believing the table can only be extended one step at a time along the arrows. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): Multiplying preserves the ratio; adding preserves the difference, which is a different invariant. Breaks: Treating adding and multiplying as two equally good ways of extending a table.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on a two row table whose first column is complete, whose top row jumps to a new value and whose cell beneath it is blank, and ask the class to say out loud what must happen to the bottom row. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Target: the blank cell in the second column. Never fill a blank before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Fill the blank cell and write the multiplier that produced it onto the arrow between the two columns. Targets: the second column and its arrow. Read the multiplier from the tool's own readout and never from this plan. Call 3. Add a column built by adding a constant to both rows instead, run the check and point at the drift printed beneath the flagged column. Targets: the added column and the drift readout. Never state the rule before the drift has appeared.

hunts: DRIFT HUNT: build a column by adding to both rows and read how far its ratio has drifted.
FRACTION JUMP: find a column whose multiplier is not a whole number and check it two different ways.
NO ARROW: hide the arrows and fill a column from a distant one, then say what multiplier you used.
PLANT ONE: build a table with exactly one bad column and let a classmate find it.

media.description: A two-row ratio table laid across the working ground, its base column pinned at the left and labelled with its own simplest form, with an arc arcing to each next column carrying the factor of change that produced it. A column earned by multiplying both entries is outlined in the primary accent and ticked; a column built by adding is flagged in the warning tone with its ratio drift printed beneath it as a number, so the failure has a measured size rather than a red mark. Cross multiplication is drawn as the two diagonals the class recognises, with its two products printed beside them, because two unequal products on screen is what refutes the additive filler and a caption is not. Every check is on the COLUMN and never on the cell, so the pair is what has to be right; the arrow label is graded separately against the operation that actually happened, and a wrong account is put up first in the warning tone and then replaced in place by the true move, which is what separates a correct number from a correct method. The factor may be a fraction and the column is still exact, drawn as a stacked numerator over a denominator rather than a decimal. Two columns with no arrow between them can be worked between, which is what stops the table being filled by stepping along a row.

scenes.valuesShown: Blackboard lines, in order: Multiplying both entries by the same number puts that number into both sides of the comparison. | It cancels between the two, so the ratio is left exactly where it was. | Adding leaves the gap between the entries the same instead of the ratio. | On a small entry a fixed amount is a large share, and on a large entry it is a small one. | So the two entries move by different proportions and the ratio drifts. concept.notation: A ratio table has two rows. A column is a pair in the ratio, and an arrow between columns is labelled with the operation that produced the second from the first.
concept.statement: A column of a ratio table stays equivalent to the base ratio only if both entries are multiplied or divided by the same number. Adding a constant to one row, or different numbers to the two rows, produces a column that is no longer in the ratio, and the drift can be measured.
prerequisites: multiplying and dividing whole numbers and fractions
misconceptions: Filling a table by continuing an additive pattern along one row.
Using different operations on the two rows, so the column is no longer in the ratio.
concept.why_it_is_true: Multiplying both entries by the same number leaves the ratio unchanged, because the multiplier cancels between the two. Adding leaves the difference unchanged instead, which is a different invariant and not the one a ratio is about. Labelling the arrow forces the operation into the open, so a right number reached by an additive route is caught.
worked_numbers: From 4 to 10 in the top row the multiplier is 2.5, so a bottom entry of 6 becomes 15.
Adding 6 to the top row instead would send 6 to 12, and the ratio drifts from 2 to 3 towards 5 to 6.
Dividing a column of 20 and 30 by 10 gives 2 and 3, which is the same ratio.

answer_key.worked: Every column must be equivalent to the base ratio, and the arrow label must name the operation that actually produced it.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn table: each correct cell as an exact fraction, the multiplier between any two columns, and whether a column is equivalent to the base.
answer_key.precision: Exact rational arithmetic throughout. Any form equivalent to the correct value is accepted, including unsimplified fractions.
answer_key.ground_truth: cellValue(base, column) = the exact rational entry. multiplier(colA, colB) = the exact ratio between them. equivalent(column, base) = cross multiplication of the two pairs.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Accepted and kept as an exact fraction, so scaling by two and a half is a legitimate move rather than an error.

edge_cases.case: A right value with a wrong arrow label
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The cell is accepted and the label is rejected, and the tool says which operation actually produced the value. A correct number reached by luck is caught here.
Flagged with the ratio drift shown numerically, so the failure is a measured change rather than a red mark.
The multiplier is not on any arrow and must be worked out, which the tool checks against the exact ratio between the two columns.
Accepted, because any form equivalent to the correct value passes. The tool notes the simplest form rather than requiring it.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

tool_config.tool_objective: The student completes a ratio table by multiplying or dividing both entries, names the operation used, and rejects row operations that break the ratio.

steps: The base ratio is 4 to 6, which reduces to 2 to 3.
