media.title: What Has to Stay Fixed
media.context: This is the chapter summary and it plays after the final topic. Every claim it makes has already been taught and practised, so nothing new appears and no fresh problem is solved. Its job is to name what stays fixed and why every method follows from it.
media.description: Ratios, simplest forms, missing terms, cross multiplication and fair sharing come together as one connected toolkit before a Binairo grid appears, where every row must balance its counts without mentioning ratios directly. The film then gathers the chapter’s central idea: a ratio compares two quantities by division, and it is the ratio, not the difference, that must remain steady for a shape or mixture to scale without changing.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Restate the chapter's conclusions about ratios, proportion, sharing, conversion and unit rates. Key teaching points: 1) A ratio compares two quantities by division. 2) Multiplying both terms preserves a ratio; adding to both does not. 3) The simplest form names every equivalent pair. 4) One known pair unlocks any other in a proportion. 5) The unit rate reduces a comparison to a single item. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often scale by adding rather than multiplying. 2) Students often solve proportions without checking the units. Pause points: 0:30, at the end of why adding fails: ask what has to stay fixed when a photo is enlarged. 1:14, just before what has to stay fixed: ask which of the four cards they would explain first. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask why adding to both parts changes a ratio. After viewing, ask what a unit rate tells you.
media.generation_prompt:
INTENT

Gather the entire ratio chapter into one connected mathematical toolkit, briefly hand that toolkit to a Binairo balancing puzzle, and then close the chapter by revealing the central idea behind all of it: a ratio compares two quantities by division, and it is the ratio, not the difference, that must stay fixed when something is scaled.

STORY

The film first gathers ratios, simplest forms, missing terms, cross multiplication and fair sharing as one connected toolkit rather than five separate tricks. A Binairo grid then appears where every row must balance its counts, even though nothing on the grid mentions ratios. The puzzle acts as a bridge back into the mathematics.

The film then gathers the chapter together. A ratio compares two quantities by division rather than subtraction. Adding the same amount to both parts changes a ratio, while multiplying both parts by the same number preserves it. The simplest form names a whole family of equivalent pairs. Once one pair is known, proportion allows another pair to be found, which supports sharing in a given ratio and unit conversion. The unit rate sharpens the comparison down to what one unit costs, covers or weighs.

The final idea is that the ratio is what has to remain steady for a shape, mixture or scaled quantity to survive without distortion. Everything else in the chapter follows from that central relationship.

RENDERER

Manim Community Edition v0.18 or later. Scene subclass.
1920x1080, 16:9, 30 fps. Default frame is 14.22 x 8 units. All content inside a 4 percent safe margin. Nothing cropped.

CHAPTER VISUAL LANGUAGE, repeat verbatim in every video of this chapter

Background: dark slate #1F2937.
Primary object / first set: teal #0072B2.
Secondary object / second set: amber #E69F00.
Shared or agreeing: green #009E73.
Focus or highlight: reddish purple #CC79A7.
Neutral construction lines, axes, ticks: grey #6B7280.
Wrong, rejected or impossible case only: muted red #D55E00.
Text off white. Body 36 px equivalent, labels 28 px.
Prose uses Text. Mathematics uses MathTex with standard LaTeX only.
Flat fills, uniform line weights, no gradients or glow.

ASSETS

No external files. No image, SVG, font or audio imports. Build everything from Manim primitives: Line, Arc, Circle, Polygon, Dot, Arrow, Brace, NumberLine, Axes, Table, VGroup.

MATHEMATICAL TRUTH MODEL

Every value below is the only value that may appear on screen.

The toolkit:
ratios, simplest forms, missing terms, cross multiplication and fair sharing.

What appears next:
a Binairo grid where every row must balance its counts.

What is asked:
to bring the whole chapter to bear on a single logic puzzle.

What a ratio is:
a comparison of two quantities by division.

What has to hold steady:
the ratio, not the difference.

Why adding fails:
adding the same amount to both parts changes a ratio, while multiplying both parts by the same number leaves the ratio unchanged.

The simplest form:
names a whole family of equivalent pairs.

What proportion buys:
one known pair unlocks any other pair.

What that handles:
sharing in a given ratio and unit conversion in the same stride.

The sharpest tool:
the unit rate, which reduces the comparison to what one of something costs, covers or weighs.

Central conclusion:
the ratio is what has to stay fixed when a quantity grows.

SCENE PLAN

Total running time 98 seconds across 7 scenes.

an empty dark slate frame.

Narration:
"So the answer to the question this chapter opened with is simply the ratio. That is what has to stay fixed when a quantity grows, and everything else in the chapter follows from it."

nothing, this is the last scene.

ANIMATION RULES

Prefer animation over narration wherever a concept can be shown.
Every scene contains at least one transformation that carries meaning.
No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
Reveal progressively; never dump a finished diagram in one Create.
On-screen text minimal; no paragraph of prose on screen at any time.
Objects that persist across scenes are transformed, never recreated.
No decorative-only animation.
The Binairo grid is a transition device and must not receive a ratio formula or worked solution.
The central ratio idea should emerge progressively after the puzzle rather than being revealed at the beginning.
Use transformations to show mathematical relationships rather than relying only on narration.

MATHEMATICAL ACCURACY, HIGHEST PRIORITY

100 percent accurate to NCERT Ganita Prakash for Class 8.
Correct notation, terminology, symbols and labels as used in the Class 8 textbook.
Proportions true wherever proportion carries meaning; if a figure is not to scale it must say so on screen.
No transformation may pass through a mathematically false intermediate state.
A ratio must be represented as a comparison of two quantities by division.
Do not imply that difference determines proportionality.
Adding the same amount to both parts must be shown as changing the ratio.
Multiplying both parts by the same number must be shown as preserving the ratio.
Equivalent ratios must reduce to the same simplest form.
Proportion must correctly connect known and unknown pairs.
Unit rate must correctly represent the comparison for one unit.
The Binairo grid must remain logically accurate and must not be presented as a ratio calculation.

LANGUAGE

British spelling.
No em dash and no en dash anywhere, in narration or on screen.
Readable aloud by a student of this grade.
Indian names and places for any person or setting if any are needed.

NEGATIVE CONSTRAINTS

No value, label or claim absent from the truth model.
No new content.
No new worked example and no extension beyond the chapter.
No text outside the safe margin.
No overlapping labels.
No external assets, watermarks or branding.
No particles, sparkles or glow.
No formula or solution is revealed in the Binairo hook.
Do not introduce a new mathematical method.
Do not add numerical examples that are not already part of the chapter.
Do not contradict the distinction between ratio and difference.
Do not introduce content beyond the stated toolkit and conclusions.

SELF-CHECK BEFORE OUTPUT

1. Scene durations sum to exactly 98 seconds across 7 scenes.
2. Every number, count and label on screen appears in the truth model and nowhere else.
3. Every mobject named in a beat is declared in the inventory before it is used.
4. Every persisting mobject is transformed into its next form, never recreated.
5. No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
6. All geometry lies within x in [-6.8, 6.8] and y in [-3.8, 3.8]; nothing is cropped.
7. No label overlaps another label; buff at least 0.2 everywhere.
8. British spelling throughout, and no em dash or en dash in narration or on screen.
9. Every idea shown has already been taught inside the chapter; nothing is new.
10. The Binairo grid appears as the connecting puzzle and contains no ratio formula or solution.
11. The final conclusion clearly states that the ratio, not the difference, is what must stay fixed under scaling.
12. The toolkit, puzzle, ratio definition, simplest form, proportion, sharing, unit conversion and unit rate all connect into one coherent chapter ending.
13. The conclusions are stated plainly and no fresh worked example appears.
14. The final frame gathers the entire chapter into the single idea that the ratio is what has to remain fixed.

media.title: Proportion Error Spotter
media.context: CBSE Class 8, Proportional Reasoning, chapter recap. Every method in the chapter is now something that can be misapplied, so this mount closes it by separating a misapplied METHOD from a slipped NUMBER. It is read after unit rate, sharing in a ratio, the multiplicative test and the non proportional cases, and it re-uses their representations for the repair replay. The class has met a : b, a/b = c/d, the unitary method with its named one unit line, cross multiplication and the sharing rule; it has NOT met slope, linear function or rate of change, and none of those words appear.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's diagnosis, the true fault kind and tag, the repaired line, and the replay that explains it.

overview.goal: The student finds the faulty step in a ratio or proportion solution, names whether it is a method or an arithmetic fault, and repairs it.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A notebook style panel on the working ground, the solution set out one step to a line, each line a tap target. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A worked solution reaches a wrong answer, and the class has to say whether the method was wrong or only the arithmetic.
overview.concept: A wrong answer in a ratio problem comes from one of two very different places. A method fault means the wrong procedure was used, such as building up additively or sharing by the number of terms. An arithmetic fault means the right method was carried out with a slip in the numbers. Telling them apart decides what has to be relearnt.
overview.purpose: The student finds the faulty step in a ratio or proportion solution, names whether it is a method or an arithmetic fault, and repairs it.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Solution fills the main panel with the kind and tag choosers beneath and the repair box under those. The replay opens to the right on a wide frame and below on a 390 px frame. Every line keeps a 44 px hit target. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not mark the faulty line while a prediction is still open, and never reveal the fault kind before it is committed. Revealing it first removes the distinction the tool is built around.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Each method fault has a signature independent of the numbers: an additive build up shows equal differences instead of equal ratios, a wrong denominator shows shares that do not add to the total, an inverted rate has the units the wrong way round, and a proportional method on a non proportional situation ignores a constant term. An arithmetic slip leaves the structure intact and only one value wrong, which is why the two can be separated by reading rather than by recomputing. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with a solution and nothing marked, and asks whether the method is wrong or only the arithmetic. Beat 2 marks the faulty line and names the fault kind, so the two sorts of error are separated. Beat 3 replays the repair on the matching representation from an earlier tool, so the correction lands where the idea came from. conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the whole solution with every line unmarked and no fault chosen, and ask the class to read it through and say out loud whether the method is wrong or only the arithmetic. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Target: the solution panel. Never mark a line or reveal the kind before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Mark the faulty line and reveal the fault kind first and then the tag, so the coarse distinction is settled before the particular error. Targets: the faulty line, the kind chooser and the tag chooser. Read the line number and the tag from the tool's own state and never from this plan. Call 3. Reveal the repair and replay it on the matching representation, so the correction lands on the tool the method came from. Targets: the repair box and the replay panel. Never restate the fault after the replay; let the corrected representation close the beat.

media.description: A worked ratio solution is set out one statement to a line in a notebook panel, each line a 44 px tap target, and beside it a drawn evidence figure whose BAR LENGTHS are the quantities. The two halves do different jobs: the notebook carries the writer's own words, and the figure settles whether the writer's rule survives being run. A fixed charge scaled as a proportion draws as a two part bar whose fixed block is visibly DUPLICATED and labelled paid twice; a total shared by the number of names draws as shares that OVERSHOOT the total bar with the sum line reading 2250 ≠ 900; an additive build up draws as two ratio pairs whose shapes differ; an inverted rate draws as a sliver on the same rupee scale beside the real per unit block. Every bar, every marker and every printed number is produced by the ONE scale function, so nothing on screen can disagree with the arithmetic behind it. In Free Play the student taps the line they would challenge, commits a fault KIND and a fault TAG, and types a repair; the three fields are graded separately, so a right kind with a wrong tag scores as partial and a repair written in an equivalent form is accepted by numeric equivalence with the tool saying that the two agree. Tapping a sound line answers with why that line holds, so a wrong tap becomes a question rather than a mark.

concept.notation: A fault kind is either method or arithmetic. A tag names the particular error within that kind.
concept.statement: A wrong answer in a ratio problem comes from one of two very different places. A method fault means the wrong procedure was used, such as building up additively or sharing by the number of terms. An arithmetic fault means the right method was carried out with a slip in the numbers. Telling them apart decides what has to be relearnt.
prerequisites: the ratio methods built in this chapter
misconceptions: All chapter errors in one bank: the additive strategy, the wrong sharing denominator, an inverted rate, and a proportional method applied to a non proportional situation.
Treating every wrong answer as an arithmetic slip.
concept.why_it_is_true: Each method fault has a signature independent of the numbers: an additive build up shows equal differences instead of equal ratios, a wrong denominator shows shares that do not add to the total, an inverted rate has the units the wrong way round, and a proportional method on a non proportional situation ignores a constant term. An arithmetic slip leaves the structure intact and only one value wrong, which is why the two can be separated by reading rather than by recomputing.
worked_numbers: Sharing 1200 in 2 to 3 by dividing by 2 gives shares that do not add to 1200, which is a method fault.
Sharing correctly but writing 240 times 2 as 460 is an arithmetic fault.
Using a proportion on a taxi fare with a fixed charge is a method fault however neat the arithmetic.

extra: A recipe scaled by adding the same number of spoons to every ingredient
A shopping bill where the unit rate was inverted before being used
A share of prize money divided by two because two people were named
A hire charge scaled as a proportion although a booking fee was paid
A currency conversion where the correct rate was multiplied out wrongly
A speed problem answered by scaling time up when it should come down
A paint mixture corrected by topping up only one colour
A correct method followed by a single multiplication slip in the last line
textbook: The journey problem solved as a proportion, which is a method fault however neat the arithmetic
The sachet and bottle prices treated as proportional to the volumes
The ages problem, where adding the same number to both terms is expected to keep the ratio
The mid day meal problem, where the factor of change has to be applied to both terms
The share problem, where the total is divided by the number of names rather than by the sum of the terms

placement.where: Closes the chapter. Every method is now something that can be misapplied, and separating a misapplied method from a slip is the assessment.

answer_key.worked: Exactly one line is at fault. The fault kind says whether the method or the arithmetic went wrong, and the tag names which error it was.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the item's own line list: the fault index, the fault kind, the tag, and whether the typed repair is numerically equivalent to the correct line.
answer_key.precision: Exact rational arithmetic for every check. Repair grading uses numeric equivalence rather than string equality.
answer_key.ground_truth: faultIndex = the single faulty line. faultKind = method or arithmetic. faultTag = the particular error. repairValid(text) = the typed line parses to the same value as the correct line.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). visual_behaviour.never: Do not mark the faulty line while a prediction is still open, and never reveal the fault kind before it is committed. Revealing it first removes the distinction the tool is built around.
visual_behaviour.scene: A notebook style panel with the solution set one step per line, each a stable tap target. The student's marked line carries the second accent; the true faulty line is revealed in the warning tone after the diagnosis. A replay panel runs the correcting representation.
visual_behaviour.layout: Solution fills the main panel with the kind and tag choosers beneath and the repair box under those. The replay opens to the right on a wide frame and below on a 390 px frame. Every line keeps a 44 px hit target.

The chosen kind and tag, once committed

animations: Line mark: the tapped line lifts slightly over 140 ms, so choosing a line is a commitment.
Kind reveal: the fault kind appears before the tag, so the coarse distinction is settled first.
Repair replay: the matching representation runs the correction, tying the repaired line to the tool the method came from.
visual_behaviour.scale_rule: Line height is derived from the panel width so every line keeps a 44 px tap target and the text stays at least 14 px; long lines wrap rather than shrinking.

mathematical_facts: A method fault means the wrong procedure was used; an arithmetic fault means the right one was carried out with a slip
A method fault has a signature that can be read without recomputing anything
An arithmetic fault leaves the structure intact and only one value wrong
A right final answer does not clear a wrong method, because the method is what is carried forward

question_integration.test: Freeze any injected step and ask: could the teacher read every number in this question off THIS screen? If not, fix the scene, not the words.
question_integration.parse_rule: Read the solution out of the question text as a list of lines, keeping the writer's own wording. Read the fault index, kind and tag from the item without revealing any of them. The solution drawn must contain every line the question supplies and no others.
question_integration.compute_rule: Build the scene from the parsed numbers, then compute the answer with the tool's own ground truth function ON THE DRAWN SCENE. Never carry the bank's answer as truth while drawing a different scene. The two must agree by construction; if they disagree the scene is wrong, not the bank.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to name the two kinds BEFORE any line is judged. The taxi solution sits on screen unmarked and the two cards say what each kind of fault is; the class is asked out loud whether the method is wrong or only the arithmetic. Naming the kinds first is what stops the whole exercise collapsing into recomputing.

Beat 2 is the argument. Line 3 is marked, the kind is named before the tag, and the green strip states that every calculation checks out while the answer is still wrong. That pairing is the lesson: a calculator cannot look where this fault lives. The figure then shows why — doubling the whole bar duplicates the 60 rupee fixed block.

Beat 3 repairs it on the same picture rather than in words: one fixed block plus a doubled variable block reaches 228, and 288 minus 228 is exactly the 60 that was counted twice. Read every number off the tool, never off this plan.

media.instructions_for_student: 1. Read the whole solution through before you touch anything. 2. Decide whether the fault is in the method or only in the arithmetic, and commit that first. 3. Tap the line you would challenge. 4. Choose the fault tag that names the particular error. 5. Type what that line should have said. 6. Submit all three and read the three grades separately. 7. Replay the repair on the representation the method came from. 8. In Practice, answer each item and press Finish when the bank is done.

media.title: Unit Rate Finder
media.context: CBSE Class 8, Proportional Reasoning - the unitary method applied to 'better buy'. The class already owns 'first find the value of ONE unit, then the value of the required number of units', and this tool is the step from describing a relationship to using one to decide something. Ratio, rate and equivalent fractions are met; constant of proportionality, reciprocal and normalisation are NOT met at this point and are never used. Reads directly onto the 1-mark 'which is better value' item and the 2-mark 'cost this many at the better rate' item.

overview.goal: The student computes a unit rate, uses it to compare two offers, and chooses which unit to compare in with a reason.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: Two horizontal tape bars on the working ground, one per offer, each labelled with its quantity and its price. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class picks the cheaper looking of two offers of different sizes, and the two bars are split to find out what one item costs.
overview.concept: Two offers of different sizes cannot be compared by their totals. Splitting each into equal parts gives the cost of one item, and the offer with the lower cost per item is better value whatever quantity is bought. The ranking does not change with quantity, which is what makes a rate the right thing to compare.
overview.purpose: The student computes a unit rate, uses it to compare two offers, and chooses which unit to compare in with a reason.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Bars stacked in the main panel with their rates beneath and the comparison panel under both. On a 390 px frame the bars keep full width and segments never fall below 12 px. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not highlight either offer while a prediction is still open or before both rates are computed, and never draw unequal segments. Unequal segments would produce a number that is not a rate.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Cost is proportional to quantity within an offer, so the cost of any amount is the unit rate times that amount. Comparing two offers at the same amount therefore comes down to comparing their unit rates, and that comparison does not depend on which amount was chosen. Changing the quantity for both offers leaves the ranking untouched, which the tool lets the student check. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): Equal value is a real answer, and the tool does not force a winner. Breaks: Believing a comparison must always name a better one. ML2 (Medium, Conceptual): A price on its own is not a rate, and only a rate compares two offers. Breaks: Comparing totals rather than rates, so the cheaper pack is called better value. ML3 (Medium, Edge Case): A rate that is not a whole number is compared exactly, never after rounding. Breaks: Believing a rate has to be a whole number before it can be used. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): The unit decides which number is larger, and never decides which offer is better. Breaks: Believing the bigger number always marks the better offer. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): The ranking is a property of the rates, which is why a rate is the right thing to compare. Breaks: Believing the better buy depends on how much is bought.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with two offers drawn as bars and both unit rates HIDDEN, and asks which looks better before any calculation. Beat 2 splits each bar into equal segments so the cost of one item appears under each. Beat 3 changes the quantity for both offers and the ranking does not move, so the rate is shown to be what decides. conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the two offer bars unsplit with both rates hidden, and ask the class to say out loud which offer looks better before any calculation. Commit the class choice on the prediction pad. Targets: both bars, unsplit. Never split a bar or show a rate before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Split each bar into as many equal segments as it has items and let the cost of one item land beneath each bar. Targets: offer A and offer B, split. Read both rates from the tool's own readouts and never from this plan. Call 3. Set a new comparison quantity so both offers are recosted, and point at the ranking indicator holding still while the bars restretch. Targets: the comparison quantity and the ranking readout. Say what stayed the same only after both totals have landed.

hunts: EQUAL VALUE: build two offers of different sizes that come out exactly equal, and say how you did it.
FLIP THE UNIT: compare a pair in items per rupee and say which number is bigger and which offer is better.
CHANGE THE AMOUNT: cost two offers at three different quantities and watch whether the ranking ever moves.
HALF RATE: build an offer whose cost per item is not a whole number and compare it without rounding.

observationsAndConclusions.why: The price of one item depends on both the quantity and the price, so a bigger pack can carry a worse rate
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The larger offer is not always the better value
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Only the rate compares offers of different sizes; the total price on its own says nothing

observationsAndConclusions.why: Cost within an offer is proportional to quantity, so both totals scale by the same amount
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Costing both offers at a different quantity leaves the ranking exactly where it was
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The ranking is a property of the rates, which is why a rate is the right thing to compare

observationsAndConclusions.why: The two units are reciprocals, so the comparison runs in the opposite direction
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Switching to items per rupee makes the larger number the better offer instead of the smaller
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The unit decides which number is bigger and never decides which offer is better

media.description: Two offers stand as measured tape bars on a working ground, and the whole lesson is in how they are drawn: a bar's WIDTH is its quantity and its HEIGHT is its unit rate, so the bar's AREA is exactly the total price. The offer that costs more in total therefore covers more ink, while the offer that is dearer PER ITEM is the taller one - which is not the longer one, so 'the bigger pack must be better' is refuted by the picture rather than by a caption. Dragging or calling splitBar cuts a bar into that many equal parts, generated from one division so every part matches to the pixel, and the first part lights up as the cost of ONE item with the rate writing itself underneath. A rate is held as an exact fraction and two rates are compared by cross multiplication on integers, so 22.5 and 22 are never allowed to tie by rounding; money prints to two decimal places and a non-terminating rate carries its exact fraction beside the decimal. Compare withholds the winner's ring until both rates actually exist, so the comparison can never be made by eye. Setting a comparison quantity recosts both offers at the SAME amount, which draws both bars at the same width and leaves only the heights - the rates - free to decide, so the ranking visibly refuses to move while the bars restretch. Switching the unit to items per rupee flips which number is larger while the highlight holds still, and the student is asked which unit they chose and why.

concept.notation: A unit rate is the cost of one item, or the number of items per rupee. Either unit can be used, but the comparison must use the same one for both offers.
concept.statement: Two offers of different sizes cannot be compared by their totals. Splitting each into equal parts gives the cost of one item, and the offer with the lower cost per item is better value whatever quantity is bought. The ranking does not change with quantity, which is what makes a rate the right thing to compare.
prerequisites: division as sharing into equal parts
misconceptions: Comparing totals rather than rates, so the cheaper pack is called better value.
Choosing the larger quantity as automatically better value.
concept.why_it_is_true: Cost is proportional to quantity within an offer, so the cost of any amount is the unit rate times that amount. Comparing two offers at the same amount therefore comes down to comparing their unit rates, and that comparison does not depend on which amount was chosen. Changing the quantity for both offers leaves the ranking untouched, which the tool lets the student check.
worked_numbers: 5 pens for 60 rupees is 12 rupees each.
8 pens for 88 rupees is 11 rupees each, so the second offer is better.
At 40 pens the first costs 480 and the second 440, the same ranking.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example recomputing at a quantity a child names and showing the ranking hold.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

visual_behaviour.never: Do not highlight either offer while a prediction is still open or before both rates are computed, and never draw unequal segments. Unequal segments would produce a number that is not a rate.
visual_behaviour.scene: Two horizontal tape bars, one per offer, labelled with quantity and price. Split segments are drawn with equal widths and tick separators, and the unit rate sits under each bar. The better offer takes the primary accent once the comparison is made.
visual_behaviour.layout: Bars stacked in the main panel with their rates beneath and the comparison panel under both. On a 390 px frame the bars keep full width and segments never fall below 12 px.
readouts: Each offer's quantity and price, always on screen
Each unit rate, once computed, as an exact fraction with any rounding rule stated
The ranking and the quantity it was checked at
animations: Split: segment separators appear left to right over 220 ms with equal spacing, so equality is seen being imposed.
Rate landing: the unit rate writes itself under the bar as the last segment lands, so the rate arrives from the split.
Quantity change: both bars restretch to the new quantity while the ranking indicator holds still, which is the invariance made watchable.
visual_behaviour.scale_rule: Bar length is proportional to quantity so the two offers are visually comparable; segments never fall below 12 px, and above 24 segments the bar shows a grouped count instead.

teaching_sequence.rationale: The split into equal parts has to be watched before the division is written, or the unit rate is a formula rather than the value of one of the pieces the bar was actually cut into

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to break the comparison the class arrives with. Both totals are on screen, 60 and 88, and the bigger total belongs to the offer that is actually the better buy - which the heights already say and the numbers do not. Do not compute a rate here and do not say the words unit rate: the beat's whole work is making 'which costs less in total' visibly the wrong question.

Beat 2 is the unitary method happening rather than being stated. Each bar divides into as many equal parts as it has items, the FIRST part lights up, and the cost of one item writes itself underneath - so the rate arrives out of the cutting rather than out of a formula. Count PARTS aloud, never separators: four parts show three lines between them, and counting the lines is the off-by-one this beat exists to pre-empt.

Beat 3 turns the observation into the reason a rate is the right thing to compare at all. Both offers are recosted at 40, which draws both bars at the SAME width, so only the heights are left to decide and the ranking cannot move. Say what stayed the same only AFTER both totals have landed, and read every number off the tool.

content.text: Two offers of different sizes cannot be compared by their totals. Splitting each into equal parts gives the cost of one item, which is the unit rate, and the offer with the lower cost per item is better value at any quantity. 5 pens for 60 rupees is 12 rupees each, while 8 pens for 88 rupees is 11 rupees each, so the second offer wins even though it costs more in total. The ranking does not change when the quantity changes, which is exactly what makes a rate the right thing to compare.
content.publication_text: Two offers of different sizes cannot be compared by their totals. Splitting each into equal parts gives the cost of one item, which is the unit rate, and the offer with the lower cost per item is better value at any quantity. 5 pens for 60 rupees is 12 rupees each, while 8 pens for 88 rupees is 11 rupees each, so the second offer wins even though it costs more in total. The ranking does not change when the quantity changes, which is exactly what makes a rate the right thing to compare.

objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what makes a picture keep its shape when it is resized through observation and reasoning, and determine that the shape is preserved only when the width and the height are multiplied by the same factor, not when the same amount is added to each. They will explain that adding 20 mm to both sides changes the shape because equal amounts are not equal factors, so comparing the width factor with the height factor predicts whether the new picture looks similar or distorted.
Examine the worked examples of same factor keeps the shape, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving same factor keeps the shape, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer what a comparison written as a : b means through observation and reasoning, and determine that a and b are its terms, that it reads as a units of the first quantity for every b units of the second, and that dividing the first term by the second tells how many times as much the first is. They will explain that a : b and b : a describe different comparisons because the order of the terms carries the meaning.
Examine the worked examples of a ratio compares two quantities, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving a ratio compares two quantities, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer what keeps two ratios describing the same relationship through observation and reasoning, and determine that multiplying or dividing both terms by the same number produces an equal ratio, while a single shared factor carries one ratio onto another. They will explain that a ratio names a multiplicative relationship preserved only when both terms are scaled by the same factor, so adding the same amount to each term breaks the equality.
Examine the worked examples of equivalent ratios by scaling, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving equivalent ratios by scaling, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer what makes a ratio as simple as it can be through observation and reasoning, and determine that dividing both terms by their highest common factor reaches the simplest form, where no whole number larger than one divides both terms. They will explain that dividing both terms by the same number keeps the comparison equal, while dividing the terms by different numbers changes the comparison and destroys the ratio.

Students will be able to infer what makes two ratios proportional through observation and reasoning, and determine that reducing each to its simplest form and checking that the forms match confirms a proportion, written as a : b :: c : d. They will explain that proportional ratios share one multiplicative relationship, so identical simplest forms prove proportion while adding the same amount to the terms does not.

Students will be able to infer what connects the two known ratios of a proportion through observation and reasoning, and determine the missing fourth term of a : b :: c : ? by finding the factor that carries the first term to the third, then multiplying the second term by that same factor. They will explain that both terms of a proportion change by one shared factor, so the missing term follows at once when that factor is known.
Examine the worked examples of the missing term by the factor of change, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving the missing term by the factor of change, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer what stays equal across a true proportion through observation and reasoning, and determine that a : b :: c : d holds exactly when a times d equals b times c, so a missing term follows by solving that equation. They will explain that the diagonal products match because both ratios share one factor of change, which makes cross multiplication a single reliable check for any proportion.

Students will be able to infer what the numbers in a sharing ratio m : n actually count through observation and reasoning, and determine that the whole splits into m plus n equal groups, so one part takes m groups and the other takes n groups. They will explain that the ratio numbers count equal groups rather than the final amounts, so the whole must first be shared into m plus n groups before either part can be found.
Examine the worked examples of sharing a whole in a ratio, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving sharing a whole in a ratio, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer why a comparison can fail when its quantities are measured differently through observation and reasoning, and determine that converting related quantities to one common unit, using standard conversions for length, mass, volume, area and time, must come before forming a proportion or finding a missing term. They will explain that a ratio compares like quantities, so a proportion is valid only when both of its ratios use the same unit.

Students will be able to infer why some paired quantities fail to change together through observation and reasoning, and determine that Celsius and Fahrenheit are not proportional because a fixed amount is added, so doubling one value does not double the other, and that speed and time for a fixed distance move in opposite directions. They will explain that a proportion applies only when two quantities change by the same factor together.
Examine the worked examples of when quantities are not proportional, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving when quantities are not proportional, across different cases.

summary_stats.counts_note: One distinct tool per concept; each tool runs four mods (AI demo, Learn, Practice, Free Play), with one objective each for AI demo, Learn and Practice and none for Free Play.
summary_stats.videos_note: One 30 to 40 second curiosity hook video per topic, plus a chapter intro video and a chapter summary video of 1 to 2 minutes each.
summary_stats.tool_needed_note: Per-item boolean for how the ANSWER is entered, NOT whether to show the tool. The frontend ALWAYS renders the tool. true = the answer must be produced through the tool. false = the student reasons it out (typed/spoken) and the tool stays on screen as an aid.
summary_stats.solved_examples_note: Each solved example carries a first-person 'reasoning' field that generalises the method.
summary_stats.practice_problems_note: 142 practice items in all = (10 microconcepts x 10 tool-answered) + (10 x 4 reasoning items) + 2 proof items on the concepts that state a general claim.
summary_stats.question_repository_note: Worked-example and practice questions are no longer inline. Each learn/practice concept carries a question_bank_ref into question_repository.json; the teacher agent pulls questions from the repository at teach time. The teaching (AI-demo) concept keeps its inline source_ai_reasoning block.

authoring_rules.nesting: Each objective contains exactly one concept; each concept contains its solved examples then its practice questions.
authoring_rules.solved_examples: At least 10 per microconcept; each is demonstrated on that section's tool with numbered steps, a final answer and first-person reasoning that models how to think, not just which buttons to press.
authoring_rules.practice_questions: At least 10 tool-answered items per microconcept (marked right/wrong on the tool), followed by exactly 4 reasoning items: application, reverse, explain, error_spotting. A concept that states a general claim carries a 5th reasoning item, proof, between explain and error_spotting.

mods.does: The AI teaches the whole concept and works the higher-order reasoning questions (application, reverse, explain, error-spotting) with full step-by-step explanations, with the tool on screen; the student only watches.
The AI demonstrates the worked examples one step at a time on the tool.
The student answers the tool-answered practice questions that reinforce the worked examples.
The student freely solves any question of the same kind on the tool, neither taught nor scored.
